title: Rabbi Zekharyah ben Avkulas
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Gittin 56b relates how Jerusalem was destroyed through Bar Kamtza, who informed the government that the Jews had rebelled against them. They sent an offering through him, and he made a blemish in it. The sages wanted to offer it for the sake of peace with the government, but Rabbi Zekharyah ben Avkulas did not let them; they wanted to kill the informer, and he did not let them. Rabbi Yochanan said of this (in Tosefta Shabbat, chapter 13 as cited by Hyman, the reading is “Rabbi Yose said,” which Hyman endorses as correct[^2]): “The humility of Rabbi Zekharyah ben Avkulas destroyed the Temple.” In [Eichah Rabbah](https://www.sefaria.org/Eikhah_Rabbah.4.3), on the verse “The sons of Zion,” Hyman reports that Rabbi Zekharyah ben Avkulas was at the feast when Kamtza expelled Bar Kamtza, and he could have protested but did not protest.[^1]
One halakhah of his is found in [Shabbat 143a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.143a.14): they said of him that he would turn his face behind the couch and throw them (the peels).

notes.text: The offering debate is at [Gittin 56a](https://www.sefaria.org/Gittin.56a.3-5), against Hyman’s 56b. Eikhah Rabbah has an unnamed host, Kamtza as his friend, and Bar Kamtza as his enemy. Its closing remark is attributed to Rabbi Yose. Hyman gives Kamtza as the host and reports the Yose attribution for Tosefta Shabbat, whose exact edition and section remain unverified.

In [Tosefta Shabbat 17:4](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Shabbat.17.4), also numbered [Tosefta Shabbat (Lieberman) 16:7](https://www.sefaria.org/Tosefta_Shabbat_%28Lieberman%29.16.7), Rabbi Yose makes the remark about Zekharyah’s humility after a description of his practice with bones and peels on Shabbat. Gittin attributes its closing remark to Rabbi Yochanan after the debate over the offering. The Tosefta wording is also attested in Eikhah Rabbah, following that work’s account of the feast.
